activities.description: Validate home blood pressure cuff accuracy and technique. Ensure readings are taken after 5 minutes of quiet rest, with back and arm supported, feet uncrossed, and cuff at heart level. Avoid measurement immediately after exercise, caffeine, or tobacco use.
activities.timing: At next visit or prior to follow-up

activities.description: Order renal function tests (e.g., serum creatinine, eGFR) and electrolytes to assess for end-organ damage associated with hypertension.
Consider lipid profile and fasting glucose/HbA1c to evaluate cardiovascular risk factors, if not recently performed.

Counsel on lifestyle modifications: limit salt intake to <5g/day, maintain healthy weight (BMI <23 kg/m²), engage in 30 minutes of daily physical activity, and avoid tobacco and excessive alcohol use.

Review medication adherence strategies for amlodipine 5 mg daily. Discuss barriers related to rotating work shifts and explore practical solutions to reduce missed doses (e.g., pill organizers, alarm reminders).
Clarify documented allergy status to ensure safety for any future medication adjustments.
Schedule follow-up appointment with general practitioner to review blood pressure control, adherence strategies, and investigation results.

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption
• Obesity | Normal | Systolic <120 AND Diastolic <80 | Reassure and encourage healthy lifestyle | | | Elevated BP | Systolic 120-139 AND/ OR Diastolic 80-89 | Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 1 | Systolic 140-159 AND/ OR Diastolic 90-99 | Pharmacological management + Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 2 | Systolic 160-179 AND/ OR Diastolic 100-109 | | | | Hypertension Grade 3 | Systolic ≥ 180 AND/ OR Diastolic ≥ 110 | | ### DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERTENSION * Systolic BP ≥140 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg on two different clinic visits * Population screening BP reading may count as the first reading * Use the higher category if only Systolic or Diastolic BP is high, manage based on the higher value * If Systolic BP is ≥160 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥100 measurement of one clinic visit is sufficient for diagnosing hypertension ### BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL TARGETS * All adults: SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg * Diabetes mellitus, CKD, or established CVD: SBP <130 and DBP <80 mmHg (optimal target if tolerated) * Age ≥80 years: SBP <150 and DBP <90 mmHg * Assess orthostatic BP at every visit of adults ≥ 65 years ---

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption
• Obesity | Normal | Systolic <120 AND Diastolic <80 | Reassure and encourage healthy lifestyle | | | Elevated BP | Systolic 120-139 AND/ OR Diastolic 80-89 | Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 1 | Systolic 140-159 AND/ OR Diastolic 90-99 | Pharmacological management + Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 2 | Systolic 160-179 AND/ OR Diastolic 100-109 | | | | Hypertension Grade 3 | Systolic ≥ 180 AND/ OR Diastolic ≥ 110 | | ### DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERTENSION * Systolic BP ≥140 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg on two different clinic visits * Population screening BP reading may count as the first reading * Use the higher category if only Systolic or Diastolic BP is high, manage based on the higher value * If Systolic BP is ≥160 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥100 measurement of one clinic visit is sufficient for diagnosing hypertension ### BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL TARGETS * All adults: SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg * Diabetes mellitus, CKD, or established CVD: SBP <130 and DBP <80 mmHg (optimal target if tolerated) * Age ≥80 years: SBP <150 and DBP <90 mmHg * Assess orthostatic BP at every visit of adults ≥ 65 years ---

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. review_notes: Patient is a 63-year-old male with established hypertension, currently on amlodipine 5 mg daily.
Recent BP is 146/88 mmHg, above the general target of <140/90 mmHg.
Lifestyle factors include high salt intake due to hostel living and limited mobility from knee discomfort.
Allergy status is unconfirmed; clarification is needed.
Lipid profile and urine albumin are unknown and should be assessed for cardiovascular risk stratification.
No acute symptoms reported; clinician disposition is routine.
draft.title: Routine Hypertension Management Plan

activities.description: Confirm current amlodipine dose, frequency, and adherence status. Verify if the patient has access to a prescription or medication packaging to confirm the exact strength.
Document allergy status explicitly. Confirm whether there are any known drug allergies, particularly to calcium channel blockers or other antihypertensives, given the current 'unconfirmed' status.
Order renal function panel (serum creatinine, eGFR, electrolytes) to assess for end-organ damage and baseline renal status before any potential medication adjustments.
Order fasting lipid profile to evaluate cardiovascular risk factors associated with hypertension.

Perform accurate clinic blood pressure measurement following standard protocol: seated, back supported, arm at heart level, after 5 minutes of rest, avoiding caffeine/tobacco for 30 minutes prior. Record exact reading without rounding.
Counsel on lifestyle modifications: limit salt intake to <5g/day, avoid tobacco and alcohol, increase physical activity to 30 minutes daily, and maintain healthy weight (BMI <23 kg/m²).
Provide guidance on home blood pressure monitoring. Recommend acquiring a validated upper-arm cuff monitor and instruct on proper technique and logging of readings for future visits.

Conduct generic medication review to assess appropriateness of current antihypertensive regimen once dose is confirmed. Evaluate for potential side effects (e.g., peripheral edema) and adherence barriers.
Schedule in-person primary care visit within the current month to review investigation results, confirm medication details, and reassess blood pressure control.

draft.title: Routine Hypertension Review and Medication Reconciliation Plan

activities.description: Interview assessment recommendation: Seek urgent care now. Assessment actions: Arrange urgent in-person clinical assessment today. Longer-term activities must not replace or delay this recommendation.

Monitor blood pressure closely during the urgent assessment. Given the patient's age (68 years), assess orthostatic blood pressure to evaluate for postural hypotension, which is relevant for safety and management planning.
Obtain recent serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) to assess renal function, as renal impairment can contribute to or result from severe hypertension.
Perform urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) or urine dipstick for proteinuria to screen for hypertensive nephropathy or underlying kidney disease.
Consider electrocardiogram (ECG) to screen for left ventricular hypertrophy or ischemic changes, given the severity of blood pressure elevation.
Review current adherence to amlodipine 10 mg daily. Verify if the patient has been taking the medication regularly and correctly, as non-adherence is a common cause of uncontrolled hypertension.
Conduct a comprehensive medication review to identify any potential drug-drug interactions, over-the-counter medications, or supplements that may exacerbate hypertension.
Counsel on lifestyle modifications including limiting salt intake to <5g/day, avoiding tobacco and alcohol, and adopting a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and healthy fats.
Advise on regular physical activity (e.g., 30 minutes daily) and weight management, if applicable, as part of long-term hypertension control.
Arrange close follow-up within 1-2 weeks after the urgent assessment to re-evaluate blood pressure control and review investigation results.
Clarify allergy status, as it is currently undocumented. Confirm any known drug allergies to ensure safe prescribing during and after the urgent assessment.
Confirm the exact timing and context of the blood pressure readings (e.g., home vs. clinic, rest period, cuff size) to ensure accuracy and rule out white-coat hypertension or measurement error.

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption
• Obesity | Normal | Systolic <120 AND Diastolic <80 | Reassure and encourage healthy lifestyle | | | Elevated BP | Systolic 120-139 AND/ OR Diastolic 80-89 | Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 1 | Systolic 140-159 AND/ OR Diastolic 90-99 | Pharmacological management + Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 2 | Systolic 160-179 AND/ OR Diastolic 100-109 | | | | Hypertension Grade 3 | Systolic ≥ 180 AND/ OR Diastolic ≥ 110 | | ### DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERTENSION * Systolic BP ≥140 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg on two different clinic visits * Population screening BP reading may count as the first reading * Use the higher category if only Systolic or Diastolic BP is high, manage based on the higher value * If Systolic BP is ≥160 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥100 measurement of one clinic visit is sufficient for diagnosing hypertension ### BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL TARGETS * All adults: SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg * Diabetes mellitus, CKD, or established CVD: SBP <130 and DBP <80 mmHg (optimal target if tolerated) * Age ≥80 years: SBP <150 and DBP <90 mmHg * Assess orthostatic BP at every visit of adults ≥ 65 years ---

scenario: Supplied urgent review for severe BP elevation

activities.description: Monitor glycemic control with HbA1c testing every 3 months given current value of 8.1% and suboptimal control, transitioning to every 6-12 months once targets are met.

Perform self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) or continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) as clinically indicated to assess pre-prandial and post-prandial levels, particularly given irregular meal patterns.
Obtain urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) to screen for diabetic nephropathy, as this is currently unrecorded.
Arrange dilated fundoscopic examination to screen for diabetic retinopathy, as the last screening date is unknown.
Assess renal function with serum creatinine and electrolytes (potassium), and obtain a fasting lipid profile to evaluate cardiovascular risk.
Perform comprehensive foot examination including peripheral pulses, monofilament testing, and inspection for ulcers or skin changes.

Provide dietary counseling focused on managing irregular meal patterns associated with night-shift work, specifically addressing the reduction of sugary tea consumption and establishing consistent carbohydrate intake.
Review current metformin therapy (500 mg twice daily) for adherence, tolerability, and efficacy in the context of persistent hyperglycemia (HbA1c 8.1%).
Document and verify allergy status, as current records indicate 'allergy status not documented' and verification is unconfirmed.
Schedule routine follow-up with general practitioner or diabetes specialist to review investigation results, adjust management plan if needed, and reinforce lifestyle modifications.

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG

Evaluate the necessity of dose adjustment or alternative therapy to mitigate hypoglycemia risk, considering the patient's age (72 years) and dietary patterns.

Obtain HbA1c to assess long-term glycemic control and inform future treatment targets, noting that higher targets may be acceptable in elderly patients with significant comorbidities.

Schedule a routine diabetes review appointment. Given the patient's preference for grouped appointments, coordinate scheduling for retinal screening and laboratory draws to occur on the same day if possible.

activities.description: Obtain urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) to assess for diabetic nephropathy progression and guide renal protection strategies.
Check serum potassium levels given CKD G3b and current losartan use to monitor for hyperkalemia risk.
Review fasting lipid profile and liver function tests (ALT, AST) as part of comprehensive metabolic assessment for diabetes and CKD.
Monitor HbA1c every 3-6 months to assess glycemic control, considering the current value of 7.8%.
Monitor blood pressure regularly, with a target of <130/80 mmHg given the presence of CKD.
Perform annual dilated fundoscopic examination to screen for diabetic retinopathy.
Perform annual comprehensive foot examination including peripheral pulses, monofilament testing, and skin inspection to screen for diabetic neuropathy and vascular disease.
Provide dietary counseling appropriate for both type 2 diabetes and CKD G3b, focusing on carbohydrate management, sodium restriction, and appropriate protein intake.

Review current medication regimen (metformin and losartan) for appropriateness given eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73 m2. Assess need for metformin dose adjustment or discontinuation based on renal function guidelines.
Review allergy status and document any known drug or food allergies, as current status is unconfirmed.
Consider referral to a renal dietitian for specialized nutritional guidance tailored to CKD G3b and diabetes.

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

review_notes: Patient has established type 2 diabetes and CKD G3b (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m2).
Current HbA1c is 7.8%, which may be acceptable depending on comorbidities and life expectancy, but requires monitoring.
Metformin use requires careful review in the context of eGFR <45 mL/min/1.73 m2; dose reduction or discontinuation may be necessary per guidelines.
Losartan is appropriate for renal protection in diabetic nephropathy but requires monitoring of potassium and creatinine.
Allergy status is currently unconfirmed and needs documentation.
Urine ACR is critical for staging diabetic kidney disease and is currently missing.
Lifestyle counseling should address both glycemic control and renal preservation.

scenario: Diabetes with established reduced kidney function

activities.description: Verify the identity, strength, and formulation of the unlabelled diabetes tablet strip brought by the patient. Confirm if the patient is currently taking this medication and if it matches any previously prescribed regimen.
Document allergy status. Confirm whether the patient has any known drug, food, or environmental allergies, as this is currently undocumented.
Order HbA1c to assess long-term glycemic control.
activities.timing: At next visit or as soon as feasible

activities.description: Order renal function tests (Serum Creatinine, eGFR) and electrolytes (Potassium) to assess kidney health and safety for diabetes medications.
activities.timing: At next visit or as soon as feasible

activities.description: Order fasting lipid profile to assess cardiovascular risk.
activities.timing: At next visit or as soon as feasible

activities.description: Order urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) to screen for diabetic nephropathy.
activities.timing: At next visit or as soon as feasible

activities.description: Order liver function tests (ALT, AST).
activities.timing: At next visit or as soon as feasible

activities.description: Measure blood pressure, BMI, and waist circumference.
Perform comprehensive foot examination including inspection of skin, nails, and assessment of peripheral pulses, monofilament sensation, and vibration sense.
Refer for dilated fundus examination to screen for diabetic retinopathy, if not performed within the last 12 months.
activities.timing: Within 12 months of last exam or at next visit if overdue

activities.description: Conduct a generic medication review once the identity of the unlabelled tablet is confirmed. Assess appropriateness of the current regimen in the context of renal function and glycemic targets. Do not adjust doses until medication identity and recent labs are verified.
activities.timing: After medication identification and lab results are available

activities.description: Counsel on diabetes self-management, including healthy eating, physical activity, and the importance of medication adherence. Discuss hypoglycemia awareness, especially if the unidentified medication is a sulfonylurea or insulin.
Schedule follow-up appointment to review laboratory results, confirmed medication list, and clinical examination findings. Adjust management plan based on these results.
activities.timing: Within 4-6 weeks or as clinically indicated

review_notes: The patient presents with established type 2 diabetes but has an unverified medication regimen. The unlabelled tablet strip poses a safety risk; identification is critical before any medication adjustments can be considered.
Allergy status is undocumented, which is a significant safety gap for prescribing any new medications or confirming existing ones.
No recent laboratory data is available. HbA1c, renal function, and lipid profile are essential for assessing current control and comorbidities.
The clinician disposition is routine, but the lack of verified medication and recent labs necessitates prompt investigation and clarification.
ICMR context (S1-S5) supports standard monitoring and investigation protocols for type 2 diabetes, including HbA1c, renal function, lipid profile, and foot/fundus exams.
Do not assume the unlabelled tablet is metformin or any other specific agent. It could be a sulfonylurea, which carries a higher risk of hypoglycemia, or another class entirely.
Ensure that any future medication changes are based on verified identity, recent lab results, and a comprehensive medication review.

activities.description: Document verified allergy status. Current record indicates 'allergy status not documented' with unconfirmed verification status.
Verify current budesonide/formoterol maintenance inhaler strength, device type, and prescribed dosing schedule. Record indicates strength and schedule are unknown.
Verify current salbutamol reliever inhaler strength and device type. Record indicates strength is unknown.
Assess and correct inhaler technique for both maintenance (budesonide/formoterol) and reliever (salbutamol) devices. Note that technique has not been assessed since a new device was supplied.
Review adherence to the budesonide/formoterol maintenance regimen. Evaluate barriers to adherence and confirm patient understanding of maintenance vs. reliever use.

Assess asthma control level using standardized criteria (e.g., daytime symptoms, night-time awakenings, activity limitation, reliever use). Current report of weekly nocturnal cough and 4 days/week reliever use suggests inadequate control.
Consider spirometry to assess pulmonary function (FEV1/PEF) if not performed recently, to establish baseline and aid in control assessment.
Develop or update a written asthma action plan. Include instructions for daily management, recognition of worsening symptoms, and steps to take during exacerbations.
Review and identify potential environmental triggers (e.g., allergens, irritants) and discuss avoidance strategies.
Schedule follow-up review in 4-12 weeks to reassess asthma control, inhaler technique, and adherence. Adjust management plan based on response.
Consider referral to a respiratory specialist if asthma remains poorly controlled despite optimized technique, adherence, and step-up therapy considerations.
activities.timing: Conditional on poor control at follow-up

### GUIDING PRINCIPLES
* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)
* Reassess at 3-4 weeks – good response: in favour of asthma diagnosis
* Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring
* Inhaler technique to be monitored
* Follow-up at 4-12 weeks, assess diseases control by clinical parameters (see Table 2)
* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### GUIDING PRINCIPLES
* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)
* Reassess at 3-4 weeks – good response: in favour of asthma diagnosis
* Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring
* Inhaler technique to be monitored
* Follow-up at 4-12 weeks, assess diseases control by clinical parameters (see Table 2)
* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

Engage the patient's daughter in device teaching and technique reinforcement to support adherence and correct usage at home.
Provide education on asthma triggers, warning signs of exacerbation, and the importance of consistent controller medication use despite variable symptoms.
Schedule follow-up review in 4-12 weeks to reassess asthma control, inhaler technique, and adherence, with potential for earlier review if symptoms worsen.
Consider referral to occupational therapy or physiotherapy for hand osteoarthritis management to improve dexterity and function for daily activities, including inhaler use.

* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)

activities.description: Obtain the complete discharge medication list, including specific inhaler products, doses, and frequencies, as these are currently unavailable.
Obtain the written asthma action plan provided at discharge, or generate a new one if unavailable.
Determine the specific trigger for the recent asthma exacerbation (e.g., viral infection, allergen exposure, non-adherence).
Document allergy status, as it is currently unconfirmed/not documented.
Reconcile the discharge inhaler regimen with current use. Verify specific products, doses, and administration technique. Ensure the patient has access to both maintenance and reliever medications.
Assess asthma control over the preceding 4 weeks, including daytime symptoms, night-time awakenings, activity limitation, and rescue inhaler use frequency.
Evaluate inhaler technique and adherence to the prescribed regimen.
Consider spirometry or peak expiratory flow (PEF) monitoring to assess baseline lung function and response to treatment, if not recently performed.
Provide patient education on asthma triggers, avoidance strategies, and the importance of adherence to maintenance therapy.
Review smoking status and advise on cessation if applicable, as smoking can worsen asthma control.
Schedule a follow-up appointment to review asthma control and adjust management if necessary, typically within 4-12 weeks post-exacerbation.
Refer to a respiratory specialist if asthma remains poorly controlled despite optimized therapy, or if there are diagnostic uncertainties.

related_icmr_context.original_text:
### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

Smoking 8 cigarettes daily is a significant risk factor for poor asthma control and exacerbations; cessation support is critical.
Medication supply interruption due to cost is a major barrier to adherence; addressing this is a priority for improving outcomes.
Allergy status is undocumented; confirmation is necessary for safe prescribing and identifying potential triggers.
Exacerbation history is unknown; this information is vital for risk stratification and determining the appropriate level of maintenance therapy.

activities.description: Interview assessment recommendation: Seek urgent care now. Assessment actions: Arrange urgent in-person clinical assessment today. Longer-term activities must not replace or delay this recommendation.

Monitor respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and ability to speak in full sentences during the urgent assessment. Watch for signs of severe exacerbation such as increased work of breathing, agitation, or desaturation.
Assess peak expiratory flow (PEF) if available, comparing to personal best if known, to help determine severity of exacerbation.
Review current budesonide/formoterol inhaler regimen details, including dose and frequency, as these are currently unavailable. Verify inhaler technique and adherence.
Clarify allergy status, which is currently undocumented, to ensure safe management and avoid potential allergen triggers.
Determine if the patient has a written asthma action plan and if they know their personal-best peak flow value.
Identify and advise on avoidance of known asthma triggers (e.g., allergens, smoke, irritants) to help prevent further exacerbations.
Schedule follow-up outpatient visit within one week after the acute episode to reassess asthma control and adjust management if needed.
Consider referral to a pulmonologist or asthma specialist if asthma remains poorly controlled despite optimized therapy or if there are frequent exacerbations.
activities.timing: Conditional on response to initial management

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### INITIATION AND MODULATION OF ASTHMA PHARMACOTHERAPY

**Flowchart:**

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

FEV1 Forced Expiratory Volume in first second, PEF Peak Expiratory Flow

---

* Inhaler technique to be monitored

* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE
ICD-10-J44.9

**WHEN TO SUSPECT?**
*   Symptoms – chronic cough, progressively worsening breathlessness
*   Risk factors – tobacco smoking, use of solid fuels for cooking, occupational exposures, Age - >35 years
*   Supportive features: Barrel shaped chest, hyperresonant note, diminished breath sounds and rhonchi on chest auscultation, forced expiratory time > 6 seconds, features of cor pulmonale (loud P2, elevated JVP, edema) in advanced cases
*   No other alternative explanation for these symptoms

**TRY AND RULE OUT**
*   Other obstructive airway disorders – Refer Asthma STW (Table 1) for features that favor COPD over asthma
*   Pulmonary tuberculosis – sputum AFB examination in case of cough ( >2 weeks)
*   Consider alternative diagnosis/- complication– presence of fever, hemoptysis, orthopnea, chest pain, significant weight loss, focal chest signs on physical examination, abnormal chest radiograph, etc.

**DIAGNOSIS & SEVERITY ASSESSMENT**
*   Airway obstruction should be documented on spirometry on all patients provisionally diagnosed as having COPD – refer if necessary. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/ FVC <0.70 defines airflow obstruction
*   Assess severity based on spirometry, severity of dyspnea (mMRC scale, Table 1), exacerbation frequency and presence of complications (see Table 2)

**TREATMENT**
*   Advice smoking cessation and counsel for other risk factors
*   Inhaled drugs are the mainstay
*   Treatment based on severity assessment (See adjacent figure)
*   Follow up: Mild to moderate disease - 3 to 6 months; Severe disease - 1-3 months
*   Ensure compliance and proper inhaler technique at each visit.
*   If uncontrolled/ complications develop, refer to higher center

**Disease progression flowchart:**
*   Disease progression -> Mild COPD
*   Disease progression -> Moderate COPD
*   Disease progression -> Severe COPD
*   Mild COPD -> Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Moderate COPD -> Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Severe COPD -> Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Mild branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Moderate branch) -> Add low dose methylxanthines
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Severe branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis

**DISEASE EXACERBATION**
**Three cardinal symptoms:**
*   Increase in dyspnea
*   Increase in sputum volume and/or
*   Increase in sputum purulence

**Classify As:**
*   Mild Exacerbation
*   Severe Exacerbation

**Features Of Severe Exacerbation:**
*   Cyanosis
*   Respiratory rate >30/ min
*   Heart rate >110/min
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   SpO2 <90%
*   Paradoxical respiratory movements
*   Altered sensorium
*   Asterixis
*   Presence of severe co-morbid conditions (e.g. heart failure, arrhythmia)

**MILD EXACERBATION**
*   Increase dose and/ or frequency of levosalbutamol and/ or ipratropium inhalation, or nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg), repeated as needed at 20-minute interval
*   Amoxycillin 500 mg TDS/ Azithromycin 500 mg OD/ Doxycycline 100 mg OD (BD on day 1) X 5 Days
*   Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily X 5 days

**SEVERE EXACERBATION**
*   Treatment as under Mild Exacerbation
*   + Supplement oxygen with target spO2 of 92% (if spO2 monitoring available)

**TABLE 1. GRADING OF BREATHLESSNESS USING MODIFIED MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL (MMRC) SCALE.**

| GRADE | DESCRIPTION OF BREATHLESSNESS |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0 | I only get breathless with strenuous exercise. |
| 1 | I get short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill. |
| 2 | On level ground, I walk slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness or have to stop for breath when walking at my own pace. |
| 3 | I stop for breath after walking about 100 yards or after a few minutes on level ground. |
| 4 | I am too breathless to leave the house or I am breathless when dressing. |

**TABLE 2. SEVERITY CLASSIFICATION FOR COPD**

| SEVERITY | POSTBRONCHODILATOR FEV1 (% PREDICTED) | DYSPNEA (MMRC GRADE) | EXACERBATIONS IN LAST ONE YEAR | COMPLICATIONS* |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| MILD | $\geq$ 80 | <2 | <2 | NO |
| MODERATE | 50-79 | $\geq$ 2 | <2 | NO |
| SEVERE | <50 | $\geq$ 2 | $\geq$ 2 | YES |

The category with the worst value should be used for severity classification
*Complications include respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, and secondary polycythemia

**RED FLAG SIGNS FOR PEOPLE HAVING EXCERBATION**
*   Altered sensorium
*   spO2 <88% despite therapy
*   Heart rate >110 bpm
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   High risk comorbid conditions (arrhythmia, congestive cardiac failure, poorly controlled diabetes, renal or liver failure)

**Refer to higher centre for further management, and ensure continued supplemental oxygen and nebulization during transfer**

**SCHEDULE FOLLOW UP VISIT ONE WEEK AFTER DISCHARGE**

Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE
ICD-10-J44.9

**WHEN TO SUSPECT?**
*   Symptoms – chronic cough, progressively worsening breathlessness
*   Risk factors – tobacco smoking, use of solid fuels for cooking, occupational exposures, Age - >35 years
*   Supportive features: Barrel shaped chest, hyperresonant note, diminished breath sounds and rhonchi on chest auscultation, forced expiratory time > 6 seconds, features of cor pulmonale (loud P2, elevated JVP, edema) in advanced cases
*   No other alternative explanation for these symptoms

**TRY AND RULE OUT**
*   Other obstructive airway disorders – Refer Asthma STW (Table 1) for features that favor COPD over asthma
*   Pulmonary tuberculosis – sputum AFB examination in case of cough ( >2 weeks)
*   Consider alternative diagnosis/- complication– presence of fever, hemoptysis, orthopnea, chest pain, significant weight loss, focal chest signs on physical examination, abnormal chest radiograph, etc.

**DIAGNOSIS & SEVERITY ASSESSMENT**
*   Airway obstruction should be documented on spirometry on all patients provisionally diagnosed as having COPD – refer if necessary. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/ FVC <0.70 defines airflow obstruction
*   Assess severity based on spirometry, severity of dyspnea (mMRC scale, Table 1), exacerbation frequency and presence of complications (see Table 2)

**TREATMENT**
*   Advice smoking cessation and counsel for other risk factors
*   Inhaled drugs are the mainstay
*   Treatment based on severity assessment (See adjacent figure)
*   Follow up: Mild to moderate disease - 3 to 6 months; Severe disease - 1-3 months
*   Ensure compliance and proper inhaler technique at each visit.
*   If uncontrolled/ complications develop, refer to higher center

**Disease progression flowchart:**
*   Disease progression -> Mild COPD
*   Disease progression -> Moderate COPD
*   Disease progression -> Severe COPD
*   Mild COPD -> Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Moderate COPD -> Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Severe COPD -> Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Mild branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Moderate branch) -> Add low dose methylxanthines
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Severe branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis

**DISEASE EXACERBATION**
**Three cardinal symptoms:**
*   Increase in dyspnea
*   Increase in sputum volume and/or
*   Increase in sputum purulence

**Classify As:**
*   Mild Exacerbation
*   Severe Exacerbation

**Features Of Severe Exacerbation:**
*   Cyanosis
*   Respiratory rate >30/ min
*   Heart rate >110/min
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   SpO2 <90%
*   Paradoxical respiratory movements
*   Altered sensorium
*   Asterixis
*   Presence of severe co-morbid conditions (e.g. heart failure, arrhythmia)

**MILD EXACERBATION**
*   Increase dose and/ or frequency of levosalbutamol and/ or ipratropium inhalation, or nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg), repeated as needed at 20-minute interval
*   Amoxycillin 500 mg TDS/ Azithromycin 500 mg OD/ Doxycycline 100 mg OD (BD on day 1) X 5 Days
*   Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily X 5 days

**SEVERE EXACERBATION**
*   Treatment as under Mild Exacerbation
*   + Supplement oxygen with target spO2 of 92% (if spO2 monitoring available)

| GRADE | DESCRIPTION OF BREATHLESSNESS |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0 | I only get breathless with strenuous exercise. |
| 1 | I get short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill. |
| 2 | On level ground, I walk slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness or have to stop for breath when walking at my own pace. |
| 3 | I stop for breath after walking about 100 yards or after a few minutes on level ground. |
| 4 | I am too breathless to leave the house or I am breathless when dressing. |

**TABLE 2. SEVERITY CLASSIFICATION FOR COPD**

| SEVERITY | POSTBRONCHODILATOR FEV1 (% PREDICTED) | DYSPNEA (MMRC GRADE) | EXACERBATIONS IN LAST ONE YEAR | COMPLICATIONS* |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| MILD | $\geq$ 80 | <2 | <2 | NO |
| MODERATE | 50-79 | $\geq$ 2 | <2 | NO |
| SEVERE | <50 | $\geq$ 2 | $\geq$ 2 | YES |

The category with the worst value should be used for severity classification
*Complications include respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, and secondary polycythemia

**RED FLAG SIGNS FOR PEOPLE HAVING EXCERBATION**
*   Altered sensorium
*   spO2 <88% despite therapy
*   Heart rate >110 bpm
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   High risk comorbid conditions (arrhythmia, congestive cardiac failure, poorly controlled diabetes, renal or liver failure)

**Refer to higher centre for further management, and ensure continued supplemental oxygen and nebulization during transfer**

*   Consider alternative diagnosis/- complication– presence of fever, hemoptysis, orthopnea, chest pain, significant weight loss, focal chest signs on physical examination, abnormal chest radiograph, etc.

1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**

2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

activities.description: Monitor weight trends and appetite status. Given the 4 kg loss over 4 months, regular weight checks are recommended to assess for further decline or stabilization.
Monitor respiratory status, including dyspnea levels (e.g., mMRC scale) and oxygen saturation, to ensure COPD remains at baseline and to detect any exacerbation early.

Investigate causes of unintentional weight loss and poor appetite. Consider basic metabolic panel, complete blood count, thyroid function tests, and inflammatory markers. Evaluate for malignancy, depression, or other systemic causes as clinically indicated.
Assess nutritional status. A formal dietary assessment is recommended to identify deficits and guide nutritional support strategies.

Refer to primary care for comprehensive evaluation of weight loss. The clinician disposition indicates a routine referral to a general practitioner to investigate the underlying cause of the 4 kg weight loss and poor appetite.
Consider referral to a dietitian or nutritionist for specialized dietary counseling, particularly given the patient lives alone and finds cooking difficult.

Address social support needs. The patient lives alone and reports fatigue affecting daily activities like cooking. Assess for community resources, meal delivery services, or home care support to assist with activities of daily living.
Encourage energy-conserving techniques and pacing of activities to manage fatigue associated with weight loss and COPD.

Review current medication regimen, specifically the tiotropium inhaler. Verify inhaler technique and adherence. Assess for any medication-related side effects that might contribute to poor appetite or weight loss. Confirm if any other medications are being used that are not recorded.

Schedule follow-up with primary care to review investigation results and adjust management plan for weight loss and COPD. Frequency should be determined by the primary care clinician based on initial findings.
Clarify allergy status. The record states 'allergy status not documented'. Confirm if the patient has any known drug or food allergies.
Clarify height. Height is missing from the record, which is needed to calculate BMI and assess nutritional status more accurately.
Clarify history of weight-loss investigations. Determine if any prior workup for weight loss has been performed.

**ADMISSION CRITERIA**
1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

activities.description: Interview assessment recommendation: Seek urgent care now. Assessment actions: Arrange urgent in-person clinical assessment today. Longer-term activities must not replace or delay this recommendation.

Monitor oxygen saturation continuously or at frequent intervals during urgent assessment. Target saturation typically 88-92% in COPD exacerbation to avoid hypercapnia, per standard guidelines. Monitor respiratory rate, heart rate, and blood pressure for signs of severe exacerbation (e.g., RR >30, HR >110, SBP <90).

Obtain chest radiograph to rule out pneumonia, pneumothorax, or other alternative diagnoses. Consider arterial blood gas analysis if respiratory distress is significant or if there is concern for hypercapnia/hypoxemia not corrected by initial measures.
Assess sputum characteristics (color, volume, purulence) to help determine etiology (bacterial vs viral) and severity. Check temperature to screen for infection.

Review current inhaler technique for tiotropium. Verify adherence to prescribed regimen. Assess for other medications that may affect respiratory status or interact with potential acute treatments. Note: Tiotropium strength is unknown in records.
Clarify complete medication list including over-the-counter drugs and supplements. Current record only lists tiotropium inhaler with unknown strength.
Clarify allergy status. Current record states 'allergy status not documented'. Essential for safe prescribing during acute management.
Clarify sputum color and presence of hemoptysis. Important for differentiating infectious causes and ruling out other pathologies.
Clarify current temperature and presence of fever. Helps assess for infectious etiology of exacerbation.

If severe exacerbation features are present (cyanosis, altered sensorium, SpO2 <88% despite therapy, hemodynamic instability), refer to higher center/ED for advanced management including possible non-invasive ventilation or intubation.
Schedule follow-up visit one week after discharge or resolution of acute exacerbation to assess recovery, review inhaler technique, and adjust maintenance therapy if needed.
Counsel on smoking cessation if applicable. Discuss avoidance of respiratory irritants and triggers. Ensure patient understands action plan for future exacerbations.

related_icmr_context.text:
Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE
ICD-10-J44.9

**WHEN TO SUSPECT?**
*   Symptoms – chronic cough, progressively worsening breathlessness
*   Risk factors – tobacco smoking, use of solid fuels for cooking, occupational exposures, Age - >35 years
*   Supportive features: Barrel shaped chest, hyperresonant note, diminished breath sounds and rhonchi on chest auscultation, forced expiratory time > 6 seconds, features of cor pulmonale (loud P2, elevated JVP, edema) in advanced cases
*   No other alternative explanation for these symptoms

**TRY AND RULE OUT**
*   Other obstructive airway disorders – Refer Asthma STW (Table 1) for features that favor COPD over asthma
*   Pulmonary tuberculosis – sputum AFB examination in case of cough ( >2 weeks)
*   Consider alternative diagnosis/- complication– presence of fever, hemoptysis, orthopnea, chest pain, significant weight loss, focal chest signs on physical examination, abnormal chest radiograph, etc.

**DIAGNOSIS & SEVERITY ASSESSMENT**
*   Airway obstruction should be documented on spirometry on all patients provisionally diagnosed as having COPD – refer if necessary. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/ FVC <0.70 defines airflow obstruction
*   Assess severity based on spirometry, severity of dyspnea (mMRC scale, Table 1), exacerbation frequency and presence of complications (see Table 2)

**TREATMENT**
*   Advice smoking cessation and counsel for other risk factors
*   Inhaled drugs are the mainstay
*   Treatment based on severity assessment (See adjacent figure)
*   Follow up: Mild to moderate disease - 3 to 6 months; Severe disease - 1-3 months
*   Ensure compliance and proper inhaler technique at each visit.
*   If uncontrolled/ complications develop, refer to higher center

**Disease progression flowchart:**
*   Disease progression -> Mild COPD
*   Disease progression -> Moderate COPD
*   Disease progression -> Severe COPD
*   Mild COPD -> Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Moderate COPD -> Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Severe COPD -> Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn
*   Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Formoterol/Budesonide (6/200 µg) as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol (50 µg) 2 puffs prn -> Persistent Symptoms
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Mild branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Moderate branch) -> Add low dose methylxanthines
*   Persistent Symptoms (from Severe branch) -> Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis
*   Add Tiotropium (9 µg) 2 puffs OD and/or low dose methylxanthines -> Refer if inadequate response, onset of new complications, or suspicion of alternative diagnosis

**DISEASE EXACERBATION**
**Three cardinal symptoms:**
*   Increase in dyspnea
*   Increase in sputum volume and/or
*   Increase in sputum purulence

**Classify As:**
*   Mild Exacerbation
*   Severe Exacerbation

**Features Of Severe Exacerbation:**
*   Cyanosis
*   Respiratory rate >30/ min
*   Heart rate >110/min
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   SpO2 <90%
*   Paradoxical respiratory movements
*   Altered sensorium
*   Asterixis
*   Presence of severe co-morbid conditions (e.g. heart failure, arrhythmia)

**MILD EXACERBATION**
*   Increase dose and/ or frequency of levosalbutamol and/ or ipratropium inhalation, or nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg), repeated as needed at 20-minute interval
*   Amoxycillin 500 mg TDS/ Azithromycin 500 mg OD/ Doxycycline 100 mg OD (BD on day 1) X 5 Days
*   Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily X 5 days

**SEVERE EXACERBATION**
*   Treatment as under Mild Exacerbation
*   + Supplement oxygen with target spO2 of 92% (if spO2 monitoring available)

**TABLE 1. GRADING OF BREATHLESSNESS USING MODIFIED MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL (MMRC) SCALE.**

| GRADE | DESCRIPTION OF BREATHLESSNESS |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0 | I only get breathless with strenuous exercise. |
| 1 | I get short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill. |
| 2 | On level ground, I walk slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness or have to stop for breath when walking at my own pace. |
| 3 | I stop for breath after walking about 100 yards or after a few minutes on level ground. |
| 4 | I am too breathless to leave the house or I am breathless when dressing. |

**TABLE 2. SEVERITY CLASSIFICATION FOR COPD**

| SEVERITY | POSTBRONCHODILATOR FEV1 (% PREDICTED) | DYSPNEA (MMRC GRADE) | EXACERBATIONS IN LAST ONE YEAR | COMPLICATIONS* |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| MILD | $\geq$ 80 | <2 | <2 | NO |
| MODERATE | 50-79 | $\geq$ 2 | <2 | NO |
| SEVERE | <50 | $\geq$ 2 | $\geq$ 2 | YES |

The category with the worst value should be used for severity classification
*Complications include respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, and secondary polycythemia

**RED FLAG SIGNS FOR PEOPLE HAVING EXCERBATION**
*   Altered sensorium
*   spO2 <88% despite therapy
*   Heart rate >110 bpm
*   Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg
*   High risk comorbid conditions (arrhythmia, congestive cardiac failure, poorly controlled diabetes, renal or liver failure)

**Refer to higher centre for further management, and ensure continued supplemental oxygen and nebulization during transfer**

**SCHEDULE FOLLOW UP VISIT ONE WEEK AFTER DISCHARGE**

**ADMISSION CRITERIA**
1. Severe symptoms; sudden worsening of resting dyspnea,
2. Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness.
3. Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management.
4. Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias, etc.)

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA**
1. Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
2. Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
3. Completion of acute medications
4. Adequate control of comorbidities

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. # Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) # HYPERTENSION IN ADULTS ### ICD-11 BA00 Hypertension is a **SILENT KILLER** as the majority of patients with high BP are asymptomatic! Only way to know if BP is high is to measure it accurately! ### BP Measurement Checklist Measure blood pressure of all adults ≥ 30 years **Illustration Description:** An illustration shows a person seated correctly for a blood pressure measurement: - **No talking during and between measurements** - **Cuff at heart level** - **Use correct cuff size and positioning** - 1. Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. Ensure cuff is on bare arm or over thin layer of clothing. Avoid bunching of clothes under cuff. - (Shows Small, Medium, Large cuff size options) - **Arm supported** - **Back supported** - **Record exact reading, don't round off** - **Legs uncrossed and feet supported** Ensure the person has not exercised, had tea/coffee, or used tobacco in the last 30 minutes. Person should rest comfortably and quietly for 5 minutes before the reading. | RISK FACTORS | CLASSIFICATION | BLOOD PRESSURE LEVELS | ACTION | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | • High salt intake
• Sedentary behavior
• Tobacco and alcohol consumption
• Obesity | Normal | Systolic <120 AND Diastolic <80 | Reassure and encourage healthy lifestyle | | | Elevated BP | Systolic 120-139 AND/ OR Diastolic 80-89 | Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 1 | Systolic 140-159 AND/ OR Diastolic 90-99 | Pharmacological management + Lifestyle modification | | | Hypertension Grade 2 | Systolic 160-179 AND/ OR Diastolic 100-109 | | | | Hypertension Grade 3 | Systolic ≥ 180 AND/ OR Diastolic ≥ 110 | | ### DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERTENSION * Systolic BP ≥140 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg on two different clinic visits * Population screening BP reading may count as the first reading * Use the higher category if only Systolic or Diastolic BP is high, manage based on the higher value * If Systolic BP is ≥160 AND/OR Diastolic BP ≥100 measurement of one clinic visit is sufficient for diagnosing hypertension ### BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL TARGETS * All adults: SBP <140 and DBP <90 mmHg * Diabetes mellitus, CKD, or established CVD: SBP <130 and DBP <80 mmHg (optimal target if tolerated) * Age ≥80 years: SBP <150 and DBP <90 mmHg * Assess orthostatic BP at every visit of adults ≥ 65 years ---

Ideal cuff bladder length is at least 80% of the person's arm circumference. - 2. Cuff should cover at least 40% of the person's upper arm. - 3. ### MANAGEMENT ALGORITHM

Sign/ symptoms suggestive of AF -> Confirm by 12 channel rhythm strip -> Hemodynamic Instability

* Hemodynamic Instability -> **Yes** -> Drug version
    * Drug version -> **Successful** -> Continue drug
    * Drug version -> **No** -> DC version
* Hemodynamic Instability -> **No** -> Very rapid HR >130/ min
    * Very rapid HR >130/ min -> **Yes** -> CHF
        * CHF -> **Yes** -> HR control Aim <110/min
            * HR control Aim <110/min -> **Careful BB/Dig Amiodarone**
            * HR control Aim <110/min -> **HR > 110/ min** -> Consider DC version
        * CHF -> **No** -> BB or Ca Block or combine
    * Very rapid HR >130/ min -> **No** -> Symptomatic
        * Symptomatic -> **Yes** -> Clinical Follow-up
        * Symptomatic -> **No** -> Clinical Follow-up

---

**Anti-coagulants in all Except**
* Reversible
* Score <1 (men) ; <2 (women)

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### LOOK FOR IMMEDIATE INTERVENTION INDICATORS:
* Systolic BP 90 mmHg, HR > 150 or <50/min
* Ongoing Angina
* CHF or TIA or stroke
* Major bleed on Oral Anti-coagulants

---

| STROKE RISK SCORE | SCORE |
| :--- | :--- |
| **CHA$_{DS}$-VASC$_{2}$** | |
| - Congestive heart failure/LV dysfunction | 1 |
| - Hypertension | 1 |
| - Aged > 75 years | 2 |
| - Diabetes mellitus | 1 |
| - Stroke/ TIA/ TE | 2 |
| - Vascular disease [prior MI, PAD or aortic plaque] | 1 |
| - Aged 65-74 years | 1 |
| - Sex category [i.e. female gender] | 1 |
| **Maximum Score** | **9** |

OAC if score >1 in men and >2 in women

| BLEEDING RISK SCORE | SCORE |
| :--- | :--- |
| **HAS-BLED** | |
| - Hypertension i.e. uncontrolled BP | 1 |
| - Abnormal renal/ liver function | 1 or 2 |
| - Stroke | 1 |
| - Bleeding tendency or predisposition | 1 |
| - Labile INR | 1 |
| - Age (e.g. >65) | 1 |
| - Drugs (e.g. concomitant aspirin or NSAIDs or alcohol | 1 |
| **Maximum Score** | **9** |

Bleeding Risk High in score >3

---

**CHOICE OF ANTI-COAGULATION:**
* Vitamin K antagonist
    * Aim for INR 2-3
* Assess risk of bleeding
* Take measures to reduce/ modify risk of bleeding
* Dietary modification & regular monitoring

**MEASURES TO REDUCE HIGH BLEEDING RISK:**
* Control SBP to less than 140 mmHg
* Avoid dietary indiscretions
* Avoid concomitant aspirin, anti platelets, NSAIDs
* Avoid alcohol
* Correct anemia

### MANAGEMENT
**AT PHC/ CHC:**
* Detailed clinical evaluation
* Basic investigations
* Careful ECG evaluation
* Start OAC if indicated (based on Stroke risk)
* Start Metoprolol if HR >110/ min & no evidence of CHF
* Refer if indicators for early intervention

**AT DISTRICT HOSPITAL:**
* Admit if indicators of early interventions
* Immediate cardioversion after heparinization, if hemodynamic instability
* Manage precipitating factors if any
* Assess stroke, bleeding risk & coagulation parameters
* Detailed echocardiogram
* Start OAC, maintain INR around 2-3
* Control HR by single drug or combination of BB & Ca Blocker
* Refer HR uncontrolled or CHF or angina

**AT TERTIARY CENTRE:**
* Re-assess clinical status, adequacy of AC
* Consider need of NOAC
* Optimise management of underlying cardiac disease
* Stress life style and AF risk factor modification
* Assess need for rhythm control and discuss pros & cons
* Consider RFA in select patient

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

## SCREENING FOR DIABETES MELLITUS

### IN AN APPARENTLY NORMAL ADULT
* In obese or overweight (BMI $\ge$ 27.5 or $\ge$ 23 kg/m²) with any of the following risk factors:
    * First degree relative with diabetes
    * History of cardiovascular disease
    * BP ($\ge$ 140/90 mmHg)
    * Dyslipidemia (TG > 250 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dl in male, <50 mg/dl in female)
    * Physical inactivity
    * Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
    * Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans)
    * Adults > 30 years of age
    * Previous history of GDM

### IN AN ADULT WITH ILLNESS
* In any adult/adolescent who presents with one of the following illness/complaints:
    * Osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, nocturia)
    * Unexplained weight loss
    * Unexplained depression or dementia
    * Acute coronary syndrome
    * Deep seated infections (liver abscess, lower lobe pneumonia, tuberculosis, pyelonephritis, abscesses, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis)
    * Recurrent infections (tinea, oral thrush, onychomycosis, cystitis-urinary tract infection, sinusitis, STI, cellulitis, carbuncle)
    * Non-healing ulcers (foot ulcers-infected/neuropathic)
    * Exogenous/iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome

### IN PREGNANCY
* H/O GDM/Pre-existing diabetes
* All pregnant women to be screened in 1st trimester with FPG
* FPG $\ge$ 126 and/or HbA1c $\ge$ 6.5% to be considered pre-existing diabetes
* FPG between 92-125 to be considered as GDM
* All those women with normal screening in 1st trimester to get a 75 g-oral glucose tolerance test done at 24-28 weeks
* All GDM women to be tested 6 weeks post-partum and once every 3 years
* PREDIABETES: should be tested yearly

### DISEASE EXACERBATION

**WHEN TO SUSPECT EXACERBATION**
* Suspect if acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80% of personal best, while on continued treatment
* Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
* If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
* Physician to assess severity of exacerbation and manage accordingly

**SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA (PATIENT TO BE ADMITTED)**
* Inability to complete sentences, agitation, use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate >30/ min, heart rate >110/ min, pulsus paradoxus >25 mm Hg, silent chest, and/ or room air sPo2 <92%
* Oxygen supplementation to maintain spO2 92-95%
* Nebulized levosalbutamol/ ipratropium (1.25 mg/ 0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
* Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Refer if no improvement
* Discharge only when symptoms improve, wheezing absent or significantly reduced, heart rate <100 bpm, respiratory rate <30/ min, room air sPo2 >94%
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**LIFE-THREATENING EXACERBATION**
* Altered sensorium, orthopnea, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, hypotension, and/ or bradycardia (heart rate <60 bpm) – immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

**NON-SEVERE ACUTE ASTHMA**
* If none of the above features present – manage on outpatient basis
* Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
* Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/ kg daily for five days
* Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

### GUIDING PRINCIPLES
* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)
* Reassess at 3-4 weeks – good response: in favour of asthma diagnosis
* Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring
* Inhaler technique to be monitored
* Follow-up at 4-12 weeks, assess diseases control by clinical parameters (see Table 2)
* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled
