### INITIATION AND MODULATION OF ASTHMA PHARMACOTHERAPY

**Flowchart:**

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

FEV1 Forced Expiratory Volume in first second, PEF Peak Expiratory Flow

### GUIDING PRINCIPLES
* Mainstay of pharmacotherapy: Inhaled drugs
* Frequency of symptoms determine treatment initiation (see figure 1 for details)
* Reassess at 3-4 weeks – good response: in favour of asthma diagnosis
* Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring
* Inhaler technique to be monitored
* Follow-up at 4-12 weeks, assess diseases control by clinical parameters (see Table 2)
* Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control (see figure 1)
* Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
* Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

### INITIATION AND MODULATION OF ASTHMA PHARMACOTHERAPY

**Flowchart:**

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

FEV1 Forced Expiratory Volume in first second, PEF Peak Expiratory Flow

# TREATMENT

### GENERAL PRINCIPLES
• Avoidance of allergens and irritant materials
• Daily bath with mild soap, keep nails short, avoid scratching
• Moisturizer are cornerstone in the management of eczema; to be applied immediately after bathing while the skin is still damp and apply multiple times during the day
• Antihistamines for (eg. levocetirizine) for control of pruritus
• Topical corticosteroids (TCS) mild – Over face/ flexures genitals. Mid potent TCS over palms, soles and lichenified lesions
• Topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs)- Face/ flexures genitals and/or as maintenance treatment
• If secondary infection (pain, pus discharge, yellow crust)- Treat with topical/ oral antibiotic as needed

### SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT
**Primary/Secondary Level**
• Treatment of active eczema: Daily use of TCS of appropriate strength until completely clear ± antihistamine (for sedative/antipruritic effects) ± oral antibiotic course (if superinfection) - (refer to STW on rational use of topical therapy)
• Maintenance treatment for area where lesions are more resistant to treatment or there is propensity for relapse, like flexural skin- Intermittent use of mid-potency TCS (e.g. 2-3 days/week) and/or TCI (e.g. 3–5 days/week)

**Tertiary Level**
• Severe disease in addition to above may require phototherapy or systemic treatment (Short course of oral corticosteroids, cyclosporine, azathioprine etc.)

***

**AVOIDANCE OF PROVOKING AGENTS, MOISTURIZERS AND EARLY TREATMENT ARE THE AIM OF ECZEMA MANAGEMENT**

activities.description: Monitor the affected skin area for signs of secondary bacterial infection, including increased pain, warmth, purulent discharge, or yellow crusting. Advise patient to seek prompt medical attention if these signs develop.

Strictly avoid further exposure to nickel. This includes avoiding the new bracelet and other potential sources such as jewelry, belt buckles, watch straps, and metal fasteners on clothing. Consider using barrier methods (e.g., clear nail polish on metal items) if avoidance is not fully possible, though removal is preferred.

Implement gentle skin care routine: Use mild, fragrance-free soap for bathing. Apply a moisturizer immediately after bathing while the skin is still damp, and reapply multiple times daily to support skin barrier function.
Avoid scratching the affected area to prevent lichenification and secondary infection. Keep fingernails short and clean.

Clinician to review current medication history. Although patient reports no current medicines, verify if any topical treatments (e.g., corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors) or oral antihistamines were used previously for this condition or are currently being used without formal prescription. Discuss appropriate use of topical therapies for symptom control if indicated.
Attend scheduled appointment with General Practitioner for routine care planning, assessment of dermatitis resolution, and discussion of long-term prevention strategies.
Confirm if the patient has undergone formal patch testing to confirm nickel allergy and rule out other concurrent allergens.
Clarify if the patient has any other known contact allergens or irritants that may contribute to dermatitis.

activities.description: Identify the active ingredients and concentration of the borrowed unlabelled cream currently in use to assess safety, potential for irritation, and appropriateness for hand dermatitis.

Review the safety and efficacy of the current unlabelled topical agent. Discuss with the patient the risks of using unidentified medications, including potential for allergic contact dermatitis to the cream itself or inappropriate potency for the affected area.

Advise on strict avoidance of identified triggers, specifically detergents. Recommend using mild, fragrance-free cleansers and wearing protective gloves (e.g., cotton-lined vinyl) when handling irritants or water.

Implement a skin barrier repair regimen: apply emollients/moisturizers frequently, especially immediately after washing hands while skin is still damp, to maintain hydration and support barrier function.
Monitor for signs of secondary bacterial infection, including increased pain, purulent discharge, yellow crusting, or spreading erythema. Advise patient to seek care if these symptoms develop.
Monitor for worsening dermatitis or lack of improvement despite trigger avoidance and emollient use. Assess for signs of systemic involvement (fever, lymphangitis), though currently denied.
Schedule routine follow-up with general practitioner to review response to trigger avoidance and emollient therapy, and to discuss appropriate prescription topical therapy if symptoms persist.

review_notes: Patient is a 58-year-old male with established hand contact dermatitis triggered by detergent use.

Patient reports using a borrowed, unlabelled cream for one week and desires increased potency; this poses a safety risk due to unknown ingredients and potential for inappropriate strength or allergens.
No systemic symptoms (fever, spreading redness, discharge) are reported, supporting routine management.

ICMR context (S1, S2) supports trigger avoidance and emollient use as cornerstone management; however, specific pharmacological interventions (e.g., topical corticosteroids) are not prescribed here per instructions, but rather framed as topics for clinician review.
The 'unknown' status of the medication statement does not negate the patient's report of using the cream; it highlights the need for clarification of its identity.
draft.title: Routine Care Plan: Hand Contact Dermatitis

activities.description: Identify the specific name, strength, and formulation of the existing prescribed skin treatment to enable accurate medication review and safety assessment.

Monitor for signs of secondary bacterial infection, including increased warmth, erythema, swelling, purulent discharge, or systemic symptoms such as fever. Advise patient to seek urgent evaluation if these red flags develop.

Strictly avoid exposure to the identified trigger (laundry soap). Use hypoallergenic, fragrance-free detergents and consider wearing protective gloves during household chores to minimize irritant contact.
Implement regular skin moisturization. Apply emollients immediately after bathing while skin is damp and multiple times daily to restore skin barrier function and reduce pruritus.

Conduct a generic review of the current topical therapy regimen. Assess adherence, application technique, and efficacy. Verify that the current treatment aligns with the severity and location of the dermatitis without prescribing specific agents or doses.

Arrange a primary-care telephone review to assess symptom persistence, review the identified medication, and adjust management plan if necessary, given the patient's inability to travel for dermatology appointments.

Consider referral to dermatology if symptoms persist despite trigger avoidance and optimized topical therapy, or if diagnosis remains uncertain. Note current travel limitations may require tele-dermatology options.

scenario: Dermatitis and limited access to skin clinic

activities.description: Monitor for the development of red-flag symptoms, including new or worsening leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction, unexplained weight loss, fever, or pain that is severe at night or unrelieved by rest. Advise patient to seek immediate medical attention if any of these occur.

Address kinesiophobia by providing written reassurance that gentle movement and walking are safe and beneficial for recovery from acute mechanical back pain. Encourage the patient to avoid prolonged bed rest and to gradually resume normal activities as tolerated.

Advise on ergonomic modifications for lifting and daily activities to reduce mechanical stress on the lower back. Suggest using proper body mechanics (e.g., bending at the knees, keeping loads close to the body) when lifting objects.

Review current use of over-the-counter analgesics or anti-inflammatory agents for pain management. Discuss appropriate usage, potential side effects, and contraindications, ensuring no interactions with any newly initiated medications.
activities.timing: At follow-up or if symptoms persist

activities.description: Schedule a follow-up review in 2 to 6 weeks if symptoms do not improve significantly, worsen, or if functional limitations persist. Earlier review is warranted if pain becomes severe or if new neurological symptoms develop.

Consider referral to physical therapy or a multidisciplinary pain management program if pain persists beyond 6 weeks, if kinesiophobia significantly impairs function, or if the patient requires structured guidance for graded activity progression.
activities.timing: Conditional on lack of improvement at 4-6 weeks

Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of HEADACHE ICD-10-G43-44

**TREATMENT FLOWCHART**
**LEGEND/ INDEX/ KEY**
* Type of Headache (Green)
* Management at PHC (Yellow)
* Management at district hospital (Dark teal)

**Flowchart Pathways:**
* CONTINUOUS HEADACHES (Progressive headache of acute or subacute onset persisting more than 1 week. Possibilities: Cerebral Venous Thrombosis, Intra Cranial Space Occupying Lesion, Meningitis, Brain abscess) -> Referred to higher centre -> [CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram, Lumbar puncture, Refer to tertiary care centre]
* CHRONIC TENSION HEADACHE (Continuous bilateral headache for many years with significant insomnia and psychosomatic complaints.) -> Start Amitriptyline (10mg HS) and advice on lifestyle -> Brain imaging if atypical features exist
* MIGRAINE (Side alternating, associated visual aura, photo-phono phobia, nausea, relieved by sleep or analgesics) -> [Frequency > 2 /month - Start prophylaxis trial for 2 months: Propranolol 40 mg OD, Flunarizine 10 mg OD; Acute management: Analgesics (Paracetamol 650 mg, or Indomethacin 50 mg) and Antiemetics (Prochlorperazine 10mg). Lifestyle changes: Good sleep at least 6 hrs, food habit modification, avoiding triggers of migraine.] -> Brain imaging if there are atypical symptoms
* ATYPICAL MIGRAINE (Hemiplegia, visual impairment, vertigo) -> Analgesics for pain, Refer to higher centre with imaging facility -> [CT/ MRI with MR angiogram or CT angiogram if required, Migraine prophylaxis after ruling out stroke and other diseases]
* TRIGEMINAL AUTONOMIC CEPHALGIAS (Rapid onset peri orbital and temporal pain with autonomic features) -> Indomethacin (25mg TID) for 7 days -> Refer to tertiary care centre
* CLUSTER HEADACHE, PAROXYSMAL HEMICRANIAS, SHORT LASTING UNILATERAL NEURALGIFORM PAIN WITH CONJUNCTIVAL INJECTION AND TEARING SYNDROME (SUNCT) -> Refer to tertiary care centre -> Refer to tertiary care centre

**RED FLAG SIGNS**
* First or worst headache of the patient's life
* Focal neurologic signs (not typical aura)
* Severe headache awakening from sleep
* Headache with fever, change in personality, mental status, level of consciousness
* Fever, neck stiffness or meningism
* New onset of severe headache in pregnancy or postpartum or while on hormone treatment
* Rapid onset with strenuous exercise
* Sudden onset (maximal intensity occurs within seconds to minutes, thunderclap headache)
* New headache type in a patient with malignancy or immunosuppression

**REASONS FOR REFERRAL**
* Non responding headaches
* Headaches with danger signs should be immediately referred and investigated for potentially dangerous conditions

**TREATMENT OF MAJOR CATASTROPHIC HEADACHES AT TERTIARY CENTRE**
* Sudden Severe headache, First or Worst headache of life -> CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram -> SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE -> Angiogram, clipping/ coiling of aneurysm (to prevent rebleed)
* Sudden Severe headache, First or Worst headache of life -> CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram -> INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE -> Stroke unit admission and neurosurgery for cortical hemorrhages or large hemorrhage with herniation
* Progressive headache -> MR venogram -> CEREBRAL VENOUS THROMBOSIS -> Intravenous UFH / subcutaneous heparin/LMWH
* Headache with fever, personality change, altered sensorium, neck stiffness -> CT scan followed by CSF study -> MENINGIOENCEPHALITIS -> Antibiotics/ antivirals
* Progressive headache with seizure or focal deficit -> CT/MRI with contrast -> BRAIN TUMORS -> Surgery, radiation, chemotherapy

**INDICATIONS FOR ADMISSION**
* Patient with unrelenting headache
* Immunosuppressed patients with continuous headache,
* First ever headache with worsening intensity,
* Progressive headache with other systemic disease
* Severe symptomatic primary headache disorders

**CRITERIA FOR DISCHARGE**
* Primary headache disorders- symptomatically improved severe episode of headache due to primary headache disorder can be discharged
* Secondary headache disorders- secondary headache disorders with essential work up, diagnosis and treatment as per individual case can be discharged

**FOLLOW UP OF HEADACHE PATIENTS**
| CAUSES OF HEADACHE | TREATMENT OF HEADACHE |
| :--- | :--- |
| Intra cerebral hemorrhage | Good control of blood pressure |
| Seizures | Antiepileptic medications |
| Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis | Follow up of anticoagulation |
| Migraine | Give prophylaxis for adequate duration of time and taper after remission |

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

draft.title: Routine Care Plan: Episodic Tension Headache

activities.description: Maintain a headache diary to track frequency, duration, intensity, and potential triggers (e.g., sleep deprivation, stress, dietary factors). Monitor for any deviation from the typical mild pressure pattern or emergence of red-flag symptoms such as sudden severe onset, neurological deficits, or fever.

Implement sleep hygiene strategies to mitigate disruption from alternating work shifts. Recommendations include maintaining a consistent sleep-wake schedule as much as possible, optimizing the sleep environment (dark, quiet, cool), and avoiding caffeine or heavy meals close to bedtime. Consider using blackout curtains and white noise machines to simulate consistent sleep conditions.

Adopt stress reduction techniques such as mindfulness, deep breathing exercises, or progressive muscle relaxation to help manage tension headache triggers. Regular physical activity, as tolerated, may also contribute to stress reduction and headache prevention.

Conduct a generic review of current and past medication use, including over-the-counter analgesics, to assess for medication-overuse headache risk. Discuss with the clinician the appropriate use of acute treatments if needed, ensuring they do not exceed recommended frequencies.

Schedule a routine visit with a general practitioner to develop a written care plan addressing headache management and sleep hygiene. Review the headache diary and assess the effectiveness of lifestyle modifications.

Clarify specific details of the alternating work shift schedule to tailor sleep hygiene recommendations more precisely. Determine if there are any specific dietary or environmental triggers identified by the patient.

activities.description: Ascertain the specific dose and frequency of paracetamol use on headache days to assess for medication overuse headache risk.
Monitor for red flag symptoms including sudden severe onset, new neurological deficits, fever, or changes in headache pattern requiring urgent evaluation.
Track headache frequency, duration, and severity to evaluate response to current management and identify triggers.
Advise on lifestyle modifications including regular sleep patterns, stress management, hydration, and identification of potential headache triggers.
Review current paracetamol use for safety, efficacy, and potential medication overuse headache; discuss general principles of acute headache management.
Schedule a primary care appointment to review headache frequency, clarify medication details, and develop a written care plan.

Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of HEADACHE ICD-10-G43-44

**TREATMENT FLOWCHART**
**LEGEND/ INDEX/ KEY**
* Type of Headache (Green)
* Management at PHC (Yellow)
* Management at district hospital (Dark teal)

**Flowchart Pathways:**
* CONTINUOUS HEADACHES (Progressive headache of acute or subacute onset persisting more than 1 week. Possibilities: Cerebral Venous Thrombosis, Intra Cranial Space Occupying Lesion, Meningitis, Brain abscess) -> Referred to higher centre -> [CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram, Lumbar puncture, Refer to tertiary care centre]
* CHRONIC TENSION HEADACHE (Continuous bilateral headache for many years with significant insomnia and psychosomatic complaints.) -> Start Amitriptyline (10mg HS) and advice on lifestyle -> Brain imaging if atypical features exist
* MIGRAINE (Side alternating, associated visual aura, photo-phono phobia, nausea, relieved by sleep or analgesics) -> [Frequency > 2 /month - Start prophylaxis trial for 2 months: Propranolol 40 mg OD, Flunarizine 10 mg OD; Acute management: Analgesics (Paracetamol 650 mg, or Indomethacin 50 mg) and Antiemetics (Prochlorperazine 10mg). Lifestyle changes: Good sleep at least 6 hrs, food habit modification, avoiding triggers of migraine.] -> Brain imaging if there are atypical symptoms
* ATYPICAL MIGRAINE (Hemiplegia, visual impairment, vertigo) -> Analgesics for pain, Refer to higher centre with imaging facility -> [CT/ MRI with MR angiogram or CT angiogram if required, Migraine prophylaxis after ruling out stroke and other diseases]
* TRIGEMINAL AUTONOMIC CEPHALGIAS (Rapid onset peri orbital and temporal pain with autonomic features) -> Indomethacin (25mg TID) for 7 days -> Refer to tertiary care centre
* CLUSTER HEADACHE, PAROXYSMAL HEMICRANIAS, SHORT LASTING UNILATERAL NEURALGIFORM PAIN WITH CONJUNCTIVAL INJECTION AND TEARING SYNDROME (SUNCT) -> Refer to tertiary care centre -> Refer to tertiary care centre

**RED FLAG SIGNS**
* First or worst headache of the patient's life
* Focal neurologic signs (not typical aura)
* Severe headache awakening from sleep
* Headache with fever, change in personality, mental status, level of consciousness
* Fever, neck stiffness or meningism
* New onset of severe headache in pregnancy or postpartum or while on hormone treatment
* Rapid onset with strenuous exercise
* Sudden onset (maximal intensity occurs within seconds to minutes, thunderclap headache)
* New headache type in a patient with malignancy or immunosuppression

**REASONS FOR REFERRAL**
* Non responding headaches
* Headaches with danger signs should be immediately referred and investigated for potentially dangerous conditions

**TREATMENT OF MAJOR CATASTROPHIC HEADACHES AT TERTIARY CENTRE**
* Sudden Severe headache, First or Worst headache of life -> CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram -> SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE -> Angiogram, clipping/ coiling of aneurysm (to prevent rebleed)
* Sudden Severe headache, First or Worst headache of life -> CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram -> INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE -> Stroke unit admission and neurosurgery for cortical hemorrhages or large hemorrhage with herniation
* Progressive headache -> MR venogram -> CEREBRAL VENOUS THROMBOSIS -> Intravenous UFH / subcutaneous heparin/LMWH
* Headache with fever, personality change, altered sensorium, neck stiffness -> CT scan followed by CSF study -> MENINGIOENCEPHALITIS -> Antibiotics/ antivirals
* Progressive headache with seizure or focal deficit -> CT/MRI with contrast -> BRAIN TUMORS -> Surgery, radiation, chemotherapy

**INDICATIONS FOR ADMISSION**
* Patient with unrelenting headache
* Immunosuppressed patients with continuous headache,
* First ever headache with worsening intensity,
* Progressive headache with other systemic disease
* Severe symptomatic primary headache disorders

**CRITERIA FOR DISCHARGE**
* Primary headache disorders- symptomatically improved severe episode of headache due to primary headache disorder can be discharged
* Secondary headache disorders- secondary headache disorders with essential work up, diagnosis and treatment as per individual case can be discharged

**FOLLOW UP OF HEADACHE PATIENTS**
| CAUSES OF HEADACHE | TREATMENT OF HEADACHE |
| :--- | :--- |
| Intra cerebral hemorrhage | Good control of blood pressure |
| Seizures | Antiepileptic medications |
| Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis | Follow up of anticoagulation |
| Migraine | Give prophylaxis for adequate duration of time and taper after remission |

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

draft.title: Routine Care Plan: Episodic Tension Headache

scenario: Frequent tension headaches and regular pain-tablet use

activities.description: Obtain current blood pressure measurement. The most recent recorded value (128/78 mmHg) is from January 2026, which is outdated for current cardiovascular risk assessment in a 63-year-old male.
Advise patient to maintain a headache diary recording frequency, duration, intensity, and potential triggers to assist in distinguishing tension-type patterns from other primary headache disorders.
Recommend non-pharmacological strategies for tension headache management, including stress reduction techniques, regular sleep hygiene, and ergonomic adjustments if work-related strain is suspected.
Encourage regular physical activity and hydration as general measures to reduce headache frequency and improve overall cardiovascular health.

Review current medication use. Patient reports no current medicines; confirm this status and discuss appropriate use of over-the-counter analgesics if needed, ensuring avoidance of medication-overuse headache.
Schedule routine follow-up with a general practitioner to monitor headache patterns, review blood pressure, and assess cardiovascular risk factors appropriate for a 63-year-old male.
activities.timing: Within 3-6 months or as clinically indicated

activities.description: Confirm absence of red-flag symptoms such as sudden severe onset, focal neurological deficits, fever, or changes in headache pattern that would warrant urgent investigation.

draft.title: Routine Care Plan: Episodic Tension Headache

scenario: Tension headache and an old BP value

activities.description: Maintain a headache diary to track frequency, duration, intensity, and potential triggers (e.g., work stress, sleep patterns, screen time). This data will assist in evaluating the effectiveness of non-pharmacological strategies.

Implement scheduled short walks and quiet breaks during busy workdays to mitigate stress-related triggers. These low-cost activities align with the patient's financial constraints and reported ability to engage in them.
activities.timing: Daily, as needed during work hours

activities.description: Prioritize consistent sleep hygiene and regular meal times to reduce physiological stressors that may exacerbate tension headaches.

Review current medication history. Although no current medicines are reported, confirm with the patient if they have used any over-the-counter analgesics or herbal supplements for headache relief, and discuss appropriate usage limits to avoid medication-overuse headache.
Schedule a routine follow-up with a general practitioner to review headache diary, assess response to lifestyle modifications, and discuss further management options if symptoms persist or worsen.

Confirm if the patient has experienced any red-flag symptoms such as sudden severe onset ('thunderclap'), neurological deficits, fever, or headaches awakening from sleep, despite previous denial. Re-assess if any new symptoms arise.

* Icon of lymph node -> Pharyngitis with generalized lymphadenopathy is consistent with **Infectious Mononucleosis(IM)**
* Icon of cigarette and reflux -> Smoking and GERD are common causes of non-infective pharyngitis

## CLINICAL EXAMINATION

**PRELIMINARY**
* Temperature chart: fever is usually absent or low-grade in viral pharyngitis
* Check for vitals/ signs of dehydration due to compromised oral intake due to odynophagia
* Complete oral and oropharyngeal examination with tongue depressor
* Palpate for cervical and generalized lymphadenopathy
* Rheumatic fever and acute glomerulonephritis are potential systemic complications of streptococcal pharyngitis
* Hepatosplenomegaly can be found in IM
* A sandpapery scarlatiniform rash may be seen in GABHS infection whereas maculopapular rashes are seen with various viral infections and with IM empirically treated with penicillin

**DESIRABLE**
Assess Centor criteria and ascertain its score

**RED FLAGS**
* Generalized lymphadenopathy
* Cardiac murmurs
* Purulent productive cough with tachypnea suggestive of LRTI
* Hot potato voice
* Unilateral tonsillar enlargement
* Tonsillar membrane going beyond its confines
* Agranulocyosis
* Epidemic of flu

**CENTOR SCORE TABLE**

| CLINICAL FEATURES | CENTOR SCORE | UNLIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | LIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | REQUIRE LAB TESTS TO CONFIRM GABHS INFECTION |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Fever | 1 | Score = 0-1 | Score = 4 | Score = 2-3 |
| Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy | 1 | | | |
| Tonsillar exudate | 1 | | | |
| Absence of cough | 1 | | | |

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of PHARYNGITIS AND SORE THROAT
### ICD-10-J02

**CLINICAL SCENARIOS**
Acute pharyngitis may include a spectrum of disease varying from simple viral pharyngitis to dreaded neck space infection.

**Clinical Scenario Timeline:**
* Icon of doctor and patient -> Acute onset of throat pain with or without – Fever, tonsillo-pharyngeal exudates, odynophagia and tender cervical lymphadenopathy is typically seen in **bacterial pharyngitis**. Streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis is the commonest cause of bacterial pharyngitis
* Icon of head with nose/eyes -> Rhinitis, conjunctivitis, skin or mucosal rashes point towards a **viral etiology**. Pharyngitis and sore throat may be the initial symptoms in epidemics of flu
* Icon of head/throat profile -> Sore throat followed by high grade fever, cough, drooling, lymphadenopathy, breathing difficulty suggest Epiglottitis or Laryngotracheobronchitis, especially in pediatric patients
* Icon of throat/tonsils -> An adherent membrane extending beyond the tonsillar confines with toxaemia suggests **Diphtheria**
* Icon of lymph node -> Pharyngitis with generalized lymphadenopathy is consistent with **Infectious Mononucleosis(IM)**
* Icon of cigarette and reflux -> Smoking and GERD are common causes of non-infective pharyngitis

activities.description: Avoid exposure to secondhand smoke and other respiratory irritants. Utilize the available option to swap tea stall locations away from the smoking area for the duration of recovery to minimize throat irritation.
Maintain adequate hydration with warm fluids (e.g., water, herbal teas) to soothe the throat and support mucosal healing. Ensure sufficient rest to facilitate immune recovery.
Monitor for resolution of sore throat and associated symptoms. Typical viral pharyngitis resolves within 7–10 days. Watch for any worsening of pain, development of high fever, or new symptoms.

Monitor for red flags indicating complications or alternative diagnoses: difficulty breathing, drooling, inability to swallow liquids, severe unilateral throat pain, or symptoms persisting beyond 10 days.

Review current use of over-the-counter symptomatic relief measures (e.g., throat lozenges, analgesics) for appropriateness and safety, considering the patient's age and lack of reported chronic medications.
Clarify documented allergy status. The record states 'Allergy status not documented'; confirm if there are any known drug or environmental allergies to ensure safe future prescribing and advice.

Re-evaluate if symptoms do not improve within 7–10 days, if they worsen, or if red flags (breathing difficulty, high fever, drooling) develop. Consider further investigation if bacterial etiology is suspected based on evolving clinical features.

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of PHARYNGITIS AND SORE THROAT
### ICD-10-J02

**CLINICAL SCENARIOS**
Acute pharyngitis may include a spectrum of disease varying from simple viral pharyngitis to dreaded neck space infection.

**Clinical Scenario Timeline:**
* Icon of doctor and patient -> Acute onset of throat pain with or without – Fever, tonsillo-pharyngeal exudates, odynophagia and tender cervical lymphadenopathy is typically seen in **bacterial pharyngitis**. Streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis is the commonest cause of bacterial pharyngitis

* Icon of throat/tonsils -> An adherent membrane extending beyond the tonsillar confines with toxaemia suggests **Diphtheria**
* Icon of lymph node -> Pharyngitis with generalized lymphadenopathy is consistent with **Infectious Mononucleosis(IM)**
* Icon of cigarette and reflux -> Smoking and GERD are common causes of non-infective pharyngitis

## CLINICAL EXAMINATION

**PRELIMINARY**
* Temperature chart: fever is usually absent or low-grade in viral pharyngitis
* Check for vitals/ signs of dehydration due to compromised oral intake due to odynophagia
* Complete oral and oropharyngeal examination with tongue depressor
* Palpate for cervical and generalized lymphadenopathy
* Rheumatic fever and acute glomerulonephritis are potential systemic complications of streptococcal pharyngitis
* Hepatosplenomegaly can be found in IM
* A sandpapery scarlatiniform rash may be seen in GABHS infection whereas maculopapular rashes are seen with various viral infections and with IM empirically treated with penicillin

**DESIRABLE**
Assess Centor criteria and ascertain its score

**RED FLAGS**
* Generalized lymphadenopathy
* Cardiac murmurs
* Purulent productive cough with tachypnea suggestive of LRTI
* Hot potato voice
* Unilateral tonsillar enlargement
* Tonsillar membrane going beyond its confines
* Agranulocyosis
* Epidemic of flu

**CENTOR SCORE TABLE**

| CLINICAL FEATURES | CENTOR SCORE | UNLIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | LIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | REQUIRE LAB TESTS TO CONFIRM GABHS INFECTION |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Fever | 1 | Score = 0-1 | Score = 4 | Score = 2-3 |
| Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy | 1 | | | |
| Tonsillar exudate | 1 | | | |
| Absence of cough | 1 | | | |

## FOLLOW UP SERVICES

Recurrent (more than 7 episodes in previuos year or 5/year in last two years or 3/year in last 3 years) tonsillitis episodes need to be evaluated for tonsillectomy.

Arrange follow-up if symptoms persist beyond typical viral course (7-10 days), worsen, or if new symptoms develop (e.g., rash, joint pain). Re-evaluate hydration status if oral intake remains poor.
Confirm documented allergy status, as current record indicates 'Allergy status not documented'.

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of PHARYNGITIS AND SORE THROAT
### ICD-10-J02

**CLINICAL SCENARIOS**
Acute pharyngitis may include a spectrum of disease varying from simple viral pharyngitis to dreaded neck space infection.

**Clinical Scenario Timeline:**
* Icon of doctor and patient -> Acute onset of throat pain with or without – Fever, tonsillo-pharyngeal exudates, odynophagia and tender cervical lymphadenopathy is typically seen in **bacterial pharyngitis**. Streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis is the commonest cause of bacterial pharyngitis
* Icon of head with nose/eyes -> Rhinitis, conjunctivitis, skin or mucosal rashes point towards a **viral etiology**. Pharyngitis and sore throat may be the initial symptoms in epidemics of flu
* Icon of head/throat profile -> Sore throat followed by high grade fever, cough, drooling, lymphadenopathy, breathing difficulty suggest Epiglottitis or Laryngotracheobronchitis, especially in pediatric patients
* Icon of throat/tonsils -> An adherent membrane extending beyond the tonsillar confines with toxaemia suggests **Diphtheria**
* Icon of lymph node -> Pharyngitis with generalized lymphadenopathy is consistent with **Infectious Mononucleosis(IM)**
* Icon of cigarette and reflux -> Smoking and GERD are common causes of non-infective pharyngitis
